newsitem.title: USA: Veto opponents denounce Supreme Court decision.
newsitem.headline: Veto opponents denounce Supreme Court decision.

text.p: President Clinton hailed the Supreme Court's decision on the line-item veto law Thursday and said he would use it wisely, but opponents predicted they would win the next time around.

"I intend to use it whenever appropriate and I look forward to using it wisely," Clinton said in a statement after the high court decided by 7-2 to throw out a challenge to the law for the time being.
The court said the six members of Congress who sued to strike down the historic line-item veto law lacked legal standing, the right to bring the case.
One of the six, New York Democratic Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, predicted that "in time the law will be challenged by persons the Supreme Court will judge to have standing."
"At that time, we are confident the court will conclude, as Justice (John Paul) Stevens did today in his dissent, that this act is unconstitutional," he said.
West Virginia Democratic Sen. Robert Byrd, another of the six, expressed disappointment but called the ruling a "temporary setback."

"Be assured that there will come a time when a state or locality, or an individual or group of individuals, will feel the brunt of the misguided legislative gimmick called the line-item veto, and will seek judicial relief," Byrd said.

Another opponent, Representative David Skaggs, a Colorado Democrat, also saw a time when the court would accept a challenge. "This is a lawsuit that someone will soon win. There are many ways to cut wasteful spending but there's only one Constitution. It prescribes the rules for making laws and the line-item veto statute violates those rules," Skaggs said.

The law empowers the president to sign a spending bill but cancel specific items including appropriations, certain tax breaks and new or expanded entitlements. Congress can override any line-item veto by a two-thirds majority in each house.

Clinton said the court's decision clears the way for the president to "use this valuable tool for eliminating waste in the federal budget and for enlivening the public debate over how to make the best use of public funds."
He said the new authority brought the government closer to the Founding Fathers' view of an effective executive role in the legislative process.

"With it, the president will be able to prevent Congress from enacting special interest provisions under the cloak of a 500- or 1,000-page bill," he said. "Special interest provisions that do not serve the national interest will no longer escape proper scrutiny."
Clinton also said the veto would provide added discipline to help balance the budget.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle called the ruling "a clear victory for the president and those of us who have supported the line item veto," adding: "I suspect that if the president has the opportunity to use it he certainly will and I can't think of a better place to start than the appropriations bills coming up."

Texas Republican Sen. Phil Gramm called the decision an important ruling "creating an essential tool for cutting waste" and added: "This ruling will give President Clinton the power to eliminate wasteful spending, and I hope that he uses that power wisely and often."
